summary: This standards-track RFC describes how Ethernet Shortest Path Bridging in MAC mode can be combined with Ethernet VPN to interwork with provider backbone bridging edges as in RFC 7623. Each attached Ethernet network is operationally isolated from the EVPN core and from the others.

plainLanguage.summary: Two different kinds of road systems need to meet at a junction. This explains how to connect them so traffic can flow without the two systems getting tangled up.

questions: connecting shortest path bridging to evpn
how does spbm work with evpn

subtitle: How islands of Shortest Path Bridging Ethernet can be joined across an EVPN core while each keeps its own control plane.

tldr.problem: Operators may have several Ethernet networks that use Shortest Path Bridging MAC mode (SPBM), plus provider backbone bridging edges, and want them to reach each other over an IP/MPLS network running Ethernet VPN (EVPN).
tldr.mechanism: A provider edge acts both as an EVPN BGP speaker and as an IS-IS SPB edge node, translating service information between the two and stripping or inserting the local backbone VLAN tag, so each island stays operationally isolated.
tldr.outcome: Different Ethernet variations get full L2 interworking through EVPN, with one designated forwarder per backbone VLAN in each island.

today: RFC 7734 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2016, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Combine SPBM and EVPN
sections.content:
This RFC describes how Ethernet Shortest Path Bridging MAC mode (SPBM), together with Provider Backbone Bridging Provider Edges (PBB PEs) and Provider Backbone Bridged Networks (PBBNs), can be supported by Ethernet VPNs (EVPNs). Each SPBM island stays operationally isolated, yet full L2 connectivity is provided between the different types of PBBNs where desired.

Each island uses its own control-plane instance and its own multipathing design, whether that is multiple equal-cost tree sets or multiple spanning trees. The stated intention is to let past, current and emerging future versions of Ethernet be interconnected, with EVPN as the unifying system. It interworks with the PBB-EVPN solution of RFC 7623.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks speak slightly different dialects of Ethernet. The goal is to let them all talk through one shared highway without forcing them to change how they work inside.

sections.title: Solution Overview
sections.content:
Each PE does control-plane interworking: it maps ISIS-SPB information (see RFC 6329) into the EVPN Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI) and back. So every such PE is both an EVPN BGP speaker and an ISIS-SPB edge node. Any number of EVPN-attached SPBM islands can be interconnected without topological or multipathing dependencies, and PBB PEs from RFC 7623 can communicate with them too.

The backbone VLAN ID (B-VID) is local to an SPBM network and is not propagated across the IP/MPLS network, so each island can configure multipathing its own way. A B-MAC tied to the B-VID is advertised with the supported I-SIDs at the PBB gateway.

Each EVPN is identified by a route target, which names the set of SPBM islands and PBB PEs allowed to communicate. Each island is given an Ethernet Segment ID (ESI) Label extended community. BGP acts as a shared repository of {B-MAC address, I-SID, Tx-Rx-attribute} tuples and distributes I-SID information into an island only on the basis of locally registered interest. If no BEB in an island has registered interest in an I-SID, information about it MUST NOT be leaked into the local ISIS-SPB routing system.

For each B-VID in an island, a single SPBM-PE MUST be elected designated forwarder (DF). It MUST strip the B-VID tag from frames relayed toward the EVPN and MUST insert the right B-VID tag into frames relayed toward the island, based on the local I-SID/B-VID bindings advertised in ISIS-SPB.
sections.plainLanguage: Each town's gate keeper translates between the town's local street names and the highway's signs. Only the one chosen gate keeper for a street does the job, and the town only hears about places its people actually want to visit.

sections.title: What a PE Is Configured With
sections.content:
At SPBM island commissioning, a PE is configured with the route target for the service instance and a unique ESI for the island. How a unique ESI is derived is out of scope.

Commissioning an ISIS-SPB node also configures a Shortest Path Source ID (SPSourceID), used to build multicast addresses algorithmically, and the set of B-VIDs used in the island with a multipathing algorithm ID for each. These can differ between domains, which is why the B-VID is local to an SPBM domain and is removed for frames carried over the IP/MPLS network. A Type 1 Route Distinguisher can be auto-derived; the procedure is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a gate opens, it gets two labels: which highway club it belongs to and a unique ID for its town. Everything else about the town stays the town's business.

sections.title: Designated Forwarder and Control-Plane Procedures
sections.content:
PEs appoint themselves DF for a B-VID in a given island using the procedure in Section 8.5 of RFC 7432. The DF originates information into BGP from ISIS-SPB and the reverse. A PE that stops being DF withdraws that information from both BGP and ISIS-SPB.

ISIS-SPB to EVPN. When a PE receives an SPBM service identifier and unicast address sub-TLV, it checks whether it is DF for the B-VID in it. If so, and the information is new or changed, it creates a MAC/IP advertisement route NLRI for each new I-SID. The Route Distinguisher is the PE's, the ESI is the island's, the Ethernet Tag ID carries the I-SID with its Tx/Rx attributes, the MAC address is copied from the sub-TLV, and a locally assigned MPLS label maps EVPN traffic to the SPBM network. The PE also keeps a table indexed by I-SID giving the B-VID, with only one entry allowed per I-SID.

EVPN to ISIS-SPB. When a PE receives new BGP NLRI, it checks whether the I-SID in the Ethernet Tag ID maps locally to a B-VID for which it is DF. If no BEB in the island showed interest in that I-SID, it is ignored. Otherwise the PE builds or updates a sub-TLV for ISIS-SPB, and uses the NLRI to fill a forwarding table indexed by B-MAC plus I-SID that points to the label stack to impose; the bottom label comes from the NLRI.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the chosen gate keeper passes messages between the town's notice board and the highway's notice board. If the gate keeper quits, it takes its notices down from both boards.

sections.title: Moving Frames Between SPBM and EVPN
sections.content:
From the island toward the EVPN: when a PE receives a frame in a B-VID for which it is DF, it looks up the B-MAC/I-SID information to find the label stack, strips the B-VID, adds the labels and forwards the resulting MPLS packet.

From the EVPN toward the island: the PE can infer the B-VID to write into the frame from the I-SID or by other means, such as the bottom label in the MPLS stack. If the frame has a local multicast destination address, the PE overwrites the SPSourceID with its local one.

Toward a PBB PE: a PBB PE has no attached PBBN and no concept of a B-VID, so no frame processing is needed. It is required to accept SPBM-encoded multicast destination addresses as if they were PBB-encoded, since only the multicast nature and the I-SID in the lower 24 bits matter.
sections.plainLanguage: When a car leaves a town, the gate takes off the town's local sticker and puts on a highway ticket. When it arrives at another town, the gate swaps the ticket for that town's sticker.

sections.title: Multicast and Transit
sections.content:
Within a PBBN, Ethernet unicast and multicast services are supported. PBB can tunnel multicast traffic in unicast PBB frames using head-end replication, and that is the only form of multicast interworking this document supports. Native PBB multicast forwarding over EVPN, PE replication and optimizing PBB multicast across the EVPN are not addressed.

A PE that does not need to take part in tandem calculations at the B-MAC layer can use the IS-IS overload bit to exclude SPBM tandem paths and act as a pure interworking platform.
sections.plainLanguage: To send one message to many people, the sender makes a separate copy for each person. A gate that does not want to carry through-traffic can say so and just do translation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Only two identifiers unique to this solution are provisioned at an SPBM-PE: the route target and the ESI. The ESI needs to be unique and common to all SPBM-PEs connected to one SPBM network or PBBN, or parts of the network will not share reachability. Cross-connecting SPBM domains by mistake, for example by provisioning the wrong route target or tying it to the wrong interface, causes black-holing or incorrect delivery with privacy issues. Consistency-checking route target provisioning when services are added or changed avoids this.

The most destructive behavior is frequent change of DF elections for an ESI, for instance when links keep going up and down. That produces heavy control-plane traffic as information is advertised and withdrawn in both SPBM and BGP. Dual-homing SPBM-PEs on both networks reduces the likelihood. Securing the BGP control plane in general is covered by the Security Considerations of RFC 4761.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone connects the wrong towns together, mail goes to the wrong place. And if the gate keeper keeps quitting and returning, everyone is kept busy updating their notice boards.

items.title: Route target
items.text: Identifies the set of SPBM islands and PBB PEs allowed to communicate.

items.title: ESI
items.text: Unique Ethernet Segment ID for each SPBM island.

items.title: B-VID
items.text: Local to each island; stripped toward the EVPN and inserted toward the island.

items.title: DF
items.text: One designated forwarder per B-VID in each island.
